import json
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path
from product_support_agent.catalog import Manifest, validate_source_url

manifest = Manifest.model_validate_json(Path("docs/operations/phase-2-product-manifest-v1.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
report = json.loads(Path("docs/operations/phase-2-ingestion-outcome-v1.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
rows = report["products"]
assert len(manifest.selected_products) == len(rows) == 100
assert report["manifest_version"] == manifest.manifest_version
assert {p.product_id for p in manifest.selected_products} == {p["product_id"] for p in rows}
assert all(validate_source_url(str(p.source_url)) for p in manifest.selected_products)
assert Counter(p["outcome"] for p in rows) == Counter(report["summary"]["outcome_counts"])
assert sum(p["attempt_count"] for p in rows) == 97
assert sum(p["outcome"] == "not_attempted" for p in rows) == 3

 for an ADR documenting the technology choices. Phase 1 implementation is

 | Ingestion outcome disclosure | Persist product-level outcomes and expose the names of successfully indexed products to demo users, with the limited-catalog disclosure. Do not imply that products without indexed sources are supported. | Approved for planning |

 The initial probe used three GETs. After additional budget approval, one more

 | [Product listing](https://my.opentext.com/support/products/) | HTTP 200, `text/html`; 3,105 bytes inspected, with no anchor or script tags in the inspected prefix | A successful HTTP status did not establish that the response contains the product catalog.  99. This evidence is inconclusive for catalog discovery, pagination, fallback
 semantics, and anonymous access to product support pages. Do not start ingestion
 until the source contract and per-run limits are verified and Phase 2 is approved.
 
 ## Proposed manifest and ingestion contract
 
 * Generate a manifest only from a successfully parsed and deduplicated catalog.
 * Store a manifest version, selection method, selected product identifiers,
   display names, canonical product URLs, and selection timestamp.
 * Reuse the same manifest for normal reruns. Replacing the sample requires an
   explicit operation and a new version.
 * Enqueue one product reference per message. Never place source content or
   credentials in queue messages.
 * Use stable source/document/chunk identifiers and content hashes for
   idempotency. Record product-level success, protected skip, retry, and failure
   outcomes without retaining protected content.
 * Treat changes to source content, parser version, embedding deployment, and
   embedding dimensions as index-versioning events.
 * Define retry, poison-message, deletion, stale-content, and partial-run behavior
   before Phase 2 implementation.

 The user approved the proposed Phase 0 direction with amendments and authorized

 authorize unrestricted crawling or bypass later phase gates.

 **Status:** Implementation complete and the Phase 2 synthetic acceptance suite
 passes 56 tests. Live source verification and the manifest outcome are pending

 # Product Support Agent #
 This repository contains a small AI-enabled application that demonstrates architecture judgment, secure production thinking, hands-on engineering depth, and the ability to move from prototype to an operable solution.
 
 ## Goal ##
 
 The Goals is to use the following URLs which contains the Product list page and the search results API page as the sources and to design and build a working AI agent (select any model) to answer questions about supported products and their resources. 
 
 1. URLs https://my.opentext.com/support/products/ and API https://my.opentext.com/api/web/support/search-results?start=1&maxResults=5&text=*. If none of these works then load from the feed https://my.opentext.com/api/web/feed/product. For each product there is a page hosted under https://my.opentext.com/support/products/{ProductCode} location where ProductCode is the "slug" property of the feed data. Each of the product support page contains knowledge articles and supporting documentations, retrieve the details from those documenation unless they are protected by authentication.
 
 2. Future requirement is to expand the agentic capability to the full support and service management system (OpenText Service Management). 
 
 3. Produce a concise architecture showing application components, identity and access, data flow, model interaction, trust boundaries, deployment, monitoring, and support ownership. 
 
 4. Document architecture decisions, security and privacy considerations, assumptions, risks, trade-offs, production-readiness gaps, and a phased path from proof of concept to production.
 
 ## Architecture Considerations ##
 
 1. I as a Senior AI Solution Architect is looking for a decoupled ingestion, Retrieval Tooling and Agentic Orchestration Architecture that would retrieve/ fetch the product listing and queries the search API with controlled pagination. It would honor the HTTP response types and act accordinlgy, as an example, if the status code is HTTP 401 then it would avoid loading the page since this demonstration should work with anonymous access alone. OpenText has multiple product knowlede/ documentations which are protected by Customer Authorization, I would skil thopse records entrirely after recording at a central place about the reason. The ingestion should run through a queue, where the entries would be loaded from the Product list, each queue item would store only one product detail, and the ingestion worker would take one item from the queue, fetch the relevant details from the supporting URLs, run the details through embedding and store it in the knowledge source. It should record the details about the operation, especially whether it is a success or failure. For this MVP I would like to select 100 products randomly from the Product list and have only those 100 ingested. I will keep the list of 100 selected product so that I can surface the names to the chat agent which will be used by the endusers during the demonstration. I would clearly indicate that this is a demo process and only the list of 100 products got ingested to avoid requiring additional infrastructure and also to avoid putting load on OpenText's infrastructure.
 2. If the product list is empty then the ingestion and normalization process would terminate. If there is a rate limitation with HTTP 429 status code then I would check for suggested retry time and perform exponential backoff before retrying.
 3. The ingestion process should normalize the results into a canonical document schema for idempotent operations and delta updates for subsequent runs.
 4. I need a hybrid search implementaion since the endusers could search with keyword/ metadata and also through semantic meanings
 5. I would keep the source URLs so that I can present the actual URL with the search results in the agent.
 6. For the agent and orchestration layer I will use an LLM with structured tool/ function calling plus retrieval augmented generation (RAG)
 7. I would enforce strict context grounding, prompt injection related defense and PII/SPI/secret redaction from logs.
 8. I don't want to show the past search histories to the enduser in this MVP but I would retail all the logs/ traces/ queries/ responses from all user sessions so that those can be reviewed later to improve the experience and detect malicious attempts.
 9. I would keep the embedding and a chat completion model behind a gateway so that I can change the models in the future without changing the code.
 10. I need every claim about a supported product or resource to map back to a retrieved source URL/ID and do not want the model to invent links or resource ever.
 11. I need to include OpenTelemetry based AI request tracing, logging and metrics, which would be sent to any capable product like Aspire or Arize Phoenix.
 12. I need an offline evaluation dataset to test factual grounding, citation accuracy etc.
 13. I would include AI Gateway, managed identity based authentication, automated build, deployment, code quality analysis, SAST, DAST and IAST validations.
 14. I also need to prepare a phased path to take this proof of concept demonstration to Production where real users can use it. This will have usability, accessibility etc. validations to ensure that I am building a product what will be helpful to the endusers and not just a working prototype that works but not useful for anyone.

 title: Product Support Agent Implementation Plan
 description: Review-gated implementation plan for a local-first product-support AI agent with a conceptual, statically validated Azure design in Canada Central
 author: Product Support Agent Team

 ## Purpose and approval model
 
 This plan turns the requirements in [Instructions.md](../Instructions.md) into a staged, testable delivery path. Phase 0, Phase 0b, and Phase 1 have been approved; implementation is limited to the current approved phase. No cloud resources or application deployments are authorized.
 
 Each phase is a separate review gate. We will not begin a phase until you approve its scope, decisions, and exit criteria. A phase is complete only after its deliverables and relevant tests pass and you approve moving on.
 
 ## Confirmed scope decisions
 
 * **Local-first demo.** The working demonstration runs locally on Podman. The MVP is complete at Phase 6.
 * **Cloud is conceptual plus IaC.** The Azure architecture (APIM, VNet, private endpoints, managed identity) exists to show the intended security posture. It is expressed as Bicep that is authored and statically validated for Canada Central (`canadacentral`). The full stack is not deployed, because APIM, AI Search, and private networking carry significant monthly cost.
 * **Network slice is deployable.** A separately deployable subset of the IaC (VNet, subnets, NSGs, egress, private DNS, and low-cost private-endpoint services) is deployed to the user-provided Azure subscription to validate routing and DNS.
 * **Models.** Chat and embedding models are Microsoft Foundry deployments supplied by the user (endpoint and deployment names), reached through LiteLLM locally. No local models are used. Credentials are never committed.
 * **Search.** Local and cloud both use the user-provided Azure AI Search service. There is no local vector store (no PostgreSQL/pgvector), which removes the local-versus-cloud adapter mismatch. The local demo therefore depends on network access to Azure.
 * **IaC modules.** Use pinned Azure Verified Modules (AVM) where available, with thin composition modules otherwise.
 * **Subscription.** The user provides an Azure subscription for `validate`, `what-if`, and the network slice.
 
 ## Product outcome
 
 Deliver a demonstrable support assistant that answers questions about a documented, explicitly selected set of 100 OpenText products. Responses must be grounded in anonymously accessible source material, cite the source URL for each product or resource claim, and clearly disclose the limited demo catalog. The architecture should provide a safe path to later customer validation and production without representing the MVP as a production service.
 
 The longer-term OpenText Service Management expansion is an architectural consideration, not MVP scope.
 
 The demo runs locally. The Azure design is presented as a validated blueprint, with an explicit statement of which security controls are demonstrated locally and which are designed only.
 
 ## Approved repository structure
 
 Use a Python `src` layout for the backend and keep application code, tests, documentation, infrastructure, and automation distinct.

 │   │   └── decisions/

 **Scope and deliverables:**
 
 * Create the approved repository structure using Python `src` layout, a TypeScript Next.js app, and the selected package boundaries. Add CODEOWNERS and an ADR template. Branch protection remains a repository-host setting that must be enabled by an authorized maintainer.
 * Document supported Python version, dependency management, formatting, linting, type checking, configuration, and local run commands.
 * Define configuration and secret handling for local development; use Podman-compatible local service orchestration.
 * Establish test conventions, fixture policy, structured logging defaults, and correlation/run identifiers.
 * Add an initial GitHub Actions validation workflow for formatting, linting, typing, unit tests, dependency checks, and secret scanning. Pin every external action to a verified full commit SHA.
 * Add a local development guide and a concise architecture overview.
 
 **Verification and exit gate:**
 
 * A clean checkout can install dependencies and run the documented checks using the approved local toolchain.
 * A small test demonstrates that configuration, logging redaction hooks, and service health checks work without real source or model credentials.
 * The validation workflow blocks merge on required checks and does not expose secrets in logs.
 * You approve the structure, developer workflow, and baseline quality gates.
 
 **Depends on:** Phase 0 and Phase 0b approval.
 
 ### Phase 2: Source catalog and resilient ingestion
 
 **Status:** The Phase 2 unit/contract suite passes 61 tests. The live OpenText
 feed returned 1,302 unique parseable products and produced the 100-product
 [manifest](./operations/phase-2-product-manifest-v1.json). The
 [source outcome report](./operations/phase-2-ingestion-outcome-v1.md) records
 97 HTTP 200 product-page responses classified as login content by the current
 heuristic and 3 products not attempted under the approved request budget. The
 page classification is not independently confirmed because response bodies
 were not retained. The live check did not enqueue messages or persist ingestion
 run records. No source content was persisted or indexed. The planned queue
 emulator integration test and Phase 2 review gate remain open. Azure AI Search
 credentials are local configuration inputs only and are not used by Phase 2
 catalog or ingestion code.
 
 **Goal:** Reliably discover the catalog and enqueue exactly the approved 100 products without exceeding source limits.
 
 **Scope and deliverables:**
 
 * Implement catalog retrieval with explicit API/feed fallback rules, response validation, controlled pagination, deduplication, and empty-catalog handling.
 * Create versioned, reproducible selection of 100 products and make the manifest available to the chat experience.
 * Enqueue one product reference per message; keep queue payloads minimal and avoid embedding content in messages.
 * Implement a worker with source host allowlisting, safe URL validation, bounded downloads, status-aware handling, `Retry-After` support, bounded exponential backoff with jitter, and dead-letter reporting.
 * Skip authenticated/protected content without attempting to bypass access controls; record a minimal reason and outcome.
 * Store run-level and product-level ingestion status with enough provenance to diagnose success, skip, retry, and failure.
 * Treat 3xx redirects to login pages and 200 responses that contain login content as protected outcomes, not only 401 and 403. Azure Storage Queue has no built-in dead-letter queue, so implement a poison queue using the dequeue count, and add run-completion tracking and partial-failure semantics.
 * Start a versioned golden evaluation set tied to the manifest version; it grows in each later phase.
 
 **Verification and exit gate:**
 
 * Unit tests cover pagination, fallback decisions, empty results, duplicate products, URL validation, status handling, retry limits, and manifest reproducibility.
 * Integration tests use a local HTTP stub and queue emulator; they do not depend on OpenText availability.
 * A controlled end-to-end run proves no more than the approved manifest is processed and no protected content is stored.
 * You approve the resulting manifest and ingestion outcome report.
 
 **Depends on:** Phase 1 approval; Phase 0 source-access and manifest decisions.
 
 ### Phase 3: Canonical documents, indexing, and hybrid retrieval
 
 **Goal:** Turn permitted source material into traceable, updateable search results.
 
 **Scope and deliverables:**
 
 * Define and version canonical document and chunk schemas, stable IDs, content hashes, provenance, and update/delete behavior.
 * Implement parsing and normalization for approved public source formats; reject unsupported or oversized content safely.
 * Define chunking, metadata filters, embedding model/version, and index schema.
 * Implement the Azure AI Search provider behind a thin retrieval/indexing interface, plus an in-memory fake used by routine unit tests. Create and version the index definition as code and apply it with a script or the SDK.
 * Implement hybrid keyword, metadata, and semantic retrieval with configurable ranking and return source IDs, URLs, and excerpts.
 * Add index reconciliation and reprocessing for changed/deleted source content.
 
 **Verification and exit gate:**
 
 * Unit tests cover normalization, canonical identity, chunk provenance, schema evolution, and idempotent updates.
 * Integration tests verify indexing, metadata filters, hybrid retrieval, source URL preservation, and deletion/reindex behavior. They run against a dedicated Azure AI Search test index as controlled live tests; routine unit tests use the in-memory fake, and CI does not require Azure Search unless approved.
 * A reviewed retrieval test set meets agreed relevance and citation-source thresholds against Azure AI Search, using a dedicated test index separate from the demo index.
 * You approve schema, freshness behavior, and retrieval quality before agent integration.
 
 **Depends on:** Phase 2 approval; Phase 0 data ownership and retrieval decisions.
 
 ### Phase 4: FastAPI and grounded agent orchestration
 
 **Goal:** Answer product-support questions with bounded tools and verifiable citations.
 
 **Scope and deliverables:**
 
 * Implement FastAPI endpoints for health, catalog availability, and chat requests using validated request/response schemas.
 * Implement the Microsoft Agent Framework orchestration and structured retrieval tool/function calling behind the approved gateway interface. Verify the framework's release status and pin its version. Chat and embedding calls go through LiteLLM to the user-provided Microsoft Foundry deployments.
 * Enforce grounding: product/resource claims must map to retrieved source IDs and URLs; do not allow the model to create or alter citations.
 * Define behavior for no results, unsupported products, ambiguous requests, model/gateway failures, and inaccessible sources.
 * Treat retrieved documents as untrusted input; apply prompt-injection defenses, tool allowlisting, output validation, and safe error handling.
 * Add request limits, timeouts, concurrency controls, and provider-independent configuration.
 
 **Verification and exit gate:**
 
 * Unit tests cover tool input/output validation, citation binding, refusal/no-result behavior, prompt-injection cases, and model/gateway failure handling.
 * Integration tests use a deterministic fake model/gateway and search provider; no live model is required for routine tests.
 * End-to-end tests prove every factual product/resource response contains valid retrieved citations and unsupported claims are not presented as facts.
 * Abuse-case tests defined in Phase 0b pass for prompt injection, exfiltration through rendered output, citation spoofing, and quota abuse, and each threat-register entry owned by this phase has its verifying test.
 * You approve representative answers and the failure/refusal experience.
 
 **Depends on:** Phase 3 approval; Phase 0 gateway, identity, and safety decisions.

 from __future__ import annotations
 
 from datetime import UTC, datetime
 from uuid import uuid4
 
 from product_support_agent.catalog import CatalogClient, CatalogOutcome, Manifest, create_manifest
 from product_support_agent.queue import InMemoryQueue
 from product_support_agent.store import IngestionRun, InMemoryIngestionStore
 
 
 class PhaseTwoService:
     def __init__(
         self,
         *,
         catalog: CatalogClient,
         store: InMemoryIngestionStore,
         queue: InMemoryQueue,
         manifest_seed: str,
         max_demo_products: int,
     ) -> None:
         self.catalog = catalog
         self.store = store
         self.queue = queue
         self.manifest_seed = manifest_seed
         self.max_demo_products = max_demo_products
         self.manifest: Manifest | None = None
         self.catalog_outcome: CatalogOutcome | None = None
 
     async def discover_and_prepare(self) -> tuple[Manifest | None, CatalogOutcome]:
         outcome = await self.catalog.discover()
         self.catalog_outcome = outcome
         if not outcome.products:
             return None, outcome
 
         manifest = create_manifest(
             outcome.products,
             manifest_version=f"demo-{datetime.now(UTC).strftime('%Y%m%d-%H%M%S')}",
             seed=self.manifest_seed,
             selection_timestamp=datetime.now(UTC).isoformat(),
             max_products=self.max_demo_products,
         )
         self.manifest = manifest
         return manifest, outcome
 
     def enqueue_manifest(self, run_id: str | None = None) -> IngestionRun:
         if self.manifest is None:
             raise RuntimeError("a manifest must be prepared before enqueueing")
         active_run_id = run_id or str(uuid4())
         now = datetime.now(UTC).isoformat()
         run = IngestionRun(
             run_id=active_run_id,
             manifest_version=self.manifest.manifest_version,
             started_at=now,
         )
         self.store.start_run(run)
         for product in self.manifest.selected_products:
             self.queue.send_product_reference(
                 active_run_id,
                 product.product_id,
                 str(product.source_url),
             )
         return run

 # Python support agent
 
 Follow the approved phase and decisions in `docs/implementation-plan.md`. Do not infer approval from a proposed architecture.
 
 * Use explicit schemas, bounded operations, typed interfaces, and errors that distinguish skips, retries, and failures.
 * Enforce source URL validation, host allowlisting, redirect checks, download limits, and bounded retries. Do not fetch protected content.
 * Keep citation IDs and URLs bound to retrieved evidence. Treat retrieved text as data, not instructions.
 * Keep provider credentials out of code, fixtures, logs, traces, and test outputs. Do not retain query or response content before privacy approval.
 * Use deterministic fakes for routine model and search tests. Exercise live services only with explicit approval and isolated resources.
 * Add focused tests for changed behavior, including relevant failure and abuse cases, and run the applicable phase checks.

 ## Approval status
 
 The user approved Phase 0 and Phase 0b, then approved Phase 1 with a requirement
 for an ADR documenting the technology choices. Phase 1 implementation is
 authorized. The demo catalog limit is parameterized with a hard maximum of 100,
 and the UI will disclose which products were successfully indexed. Query and
 response retention must remain disabled until the privacy and provider-handling
 conditions are approved. Cloud resource creation and application deployment
 remain unauthorized. Source verification and later phase gates remain
 prerequisites for ingestion.
 
 The user approved the Phase 0b [threat register](../security/threat-register.md)
 and [privacy impact assessment](../security/privacy-impact-assessment.md) with
 conditions. Query/response retention remains disabled until provider handling,
 reviewer access, notice, redaction, TTL, and deletion are verified.
 
 ## Decisions requiring review
 
 | Topic | Proposed decision | Status |
 |---|---|---|
 | Product users and tasks | Target support engineers and product support analysts. Cover five tasks: confirm a product is in the demo catalog, find a public resource, answer a product question with a citation, explain when no indexed source exists, and identify an unsupported request. Proposed usability bar: at least four of five representative users complete at least four of these five tasks without moderator help. | Approved for planning; usability evidence remains Phase 5 |
 | Anonymous source access | Fetch only explicitly allowlisted OpenText hosts with anonymous GET requests. Never submit credentials or bypass a 401/403. Identify login redirects and login content as protected outcomes. | Approved; source terms and catalog behavior still require verification |
 | Catalog fallback | Use the feed only when the listing and search API cannot provide a valid catalog. Distinguish authorization failures, malformed responses, and empty catalogs. | Feed parsed successfully; product-page access remains inconclusive |
 | Source request budget | The user authorized up to 100 additional GET requests for bounded source verification/ingestion; one was previously used for a bounded feed-prefix check. This is not permission for unrestricted crawling. | Original 100-GET cap exhausted; one separately authorized full-feed GET was also used. Further GETs require approval. |
 | 100-product manifest | Use `MAX_DEMO_PRODUCTS`, default 100 and hard maximum 100. Select randomly once per manifest version, persist exact product IDs/names/URLs, and reuse for reruns. Sample from the full catalog; report products with no permitted indexed sources. | Live manifest generated; user review and approval pending |
 | Ingestion outcome disclosure | Persist product-level outcomes and expose the names of successfully indexed products to demo users, with the limited-catalog disclosure. Do not imply that products without indexed sources are supported. | Approved for planning |
 | Data ownership | MongoDB is the system of record for manifests, run/product outcomes, and canonical documents. Azure AI Search is a derived index of traceable chunks. Queue messages carry product references only. | Approved for planning |
 | Search | Use the same user-provided Azure AI Search service locally and in the cloud design. Keep a thin interface and in-memory fake for routine tests. Use hybrid text/vector retrieval and preserve metadata filters and provenance. | Approved for planning; endpoint access remains user-provided |
 | Search ranking | Start with Azure AI Search hybrid retrieval. Decide semantic reranking, fields, filters, and acceptance thresholds using a reviewed test set before Phase 3 closes. | Approved direction; details remain for Phase 3 |
 | Local component boundaries | Run the Next.js frontend, FastAPI with the agent, ingestion worker, LiteLLM, MongoDB, and Azurite as separate local Podman services. Keep the catalog process as a bounded worker/command using the same ingestion package. | Approved; foundation created. MongoDB and Azurite Podman runtime verified on 2026-11-21 (see [local development](../operations/local-development.md#podman-verification-record)); application services are containerized in later phases |
 | User-interface and backend languages | Use React/Next.js with TypeScript and Python with FastAPI/Microsoft Agent Framework. Record why these choices fit the project and document their toolchain trade-offs in [ADR-0005](decisions/adr-0005-ui-and-backend-technology.md). | Approved for Phase 1 |
 | Model gateway | Route chat and embedding requests through local LiteLLM to the user's Foundry deployments. Keep endpoint/deployment configuration outside source control and verify protocol compatibility before Phase 4. | Approved direction; protocol verification remains Phase 4 |
 | Citation handling | Retrieval returns stable evidence IDs and source URLs. The model may refer only to evidence IDs; the server resolves IDs to canonical URLs and renders citations. Never accept model-authored URLs as citations. | Approved for planning |
 | User authentication | No end-user authentication in the local MVP. Bind the demo to a local interface and do not expose it as a public service. Cloud authentication remains design-only for Phase 7. | Approved for planning |
 | Query and response telemetry | The user requests demo query/response retention. Use `QUERY_RESPONSE_RETENTION_ENABLED=false` by default, a per-session opt-out, `QUERY_RESPONSE_RETENTION_DAYS=7` as a configurable default, and a parameterized reviewer role. Do not retain real content until policy, provider handling, notice, access, redaction, retention, and deletion controls are approved. | Phase 0b design approved; implementation remains gated |
 | Chat history | Do not display past searches in the MVP. Keep any UI session state transient and document its behavior. | Approved for planning |
 | Evaluation | Version a synthetic/reviewed dataset. Proposed gates: 100% of displayed citations resolve to retrieved evidence; zero unsupported product/resource claims in the reviewed set; relevant evidence appears in the top five results for at least 90% of reviewed questions. Agree on latency and cost targets before Phase 6. | Approved for planning; latency and cost targets remain open |
 | Accessibility | Target WCAG 2.2 AA, with automated checks plus manual keyboard and screen-reader review before Phase 5 closes. | Approved for planning |
 | Caching | No cache in the MVP. Revisit only if baseline measurements show a need and cache data, TTL, and invalidation are approved. | Approved for planning |
 | Azure deployment | Keep the application stack conceptual and statically validated only. Do not deploy APIM, AI Search, Cosmos DB, Container Apps, or application workloads. Review the separately deployable network slice only in Phase 7. | Approved for planning |
 
 ## Source verification
 
 The initial probe used three GETs. After additional budget approval, one more
 GET was used to read a bounded feed prefix. Redirects were not followed, and no
 response body was stored.
 
 | Endpoint | Result | Interpretation |
 |---|---|---|
 | [Product listing](https://my.opentext.com/support/products/) | HTTP 200, `text/html`; 3,105 bytes inspected, with no anchor or script tags in the inspected prefix | A successful HTTP status did not establish that the response contains the product catalog. Server-rendering and page semantics remain unverified. |
 | [Search results API](https://my.opentext.com/api/web/support/search-results?start=1&maxResults=5&text=%2A) | HTTP 401, `text/plain` | Treat this API response as protected. Do not retry with credentials or treat it as an empty catalog. |
 | [Product feed](https://my.opentext.com/api/web/feed/product) | HTTP 200, `application/json`; an additional bounded read reached 16,385 bytes and was truncated | The complete feed was not downloaded or parsed. The response is larger than the probe limit; pagination, size, and parsing remain unverified. No response body was retained. |
 
 The initial probe used three GETs. Of the original 100 additional GETs, one was
 previously used for a bounded feed-prefix read. The live verification used two
 feed GETs and 97 product-page GETs, exhausting that original additional budget.
 The user separately authorized one full-feed GET, which was also used in this
 verification. This accounts for 100 GETs under the original additional cap plus
 one separately authorized full-feed GET; the cumulative count including the
 initial three probes is 104.
 
 The full feed parsed into 1,302 unique products and produced the
 [100-product manifest](../operations/phase-2-product-manifest-v1.json). Of the
 97 product pages checked, all returned HTTP 200 but the login-content heuristic
 classified them as protected. Three manifest products were not checked. Since
 response bodies were not retained, those classifications are inconclusive. The
 [outcome report](../operations/phase-2-ingestion-outcome-v1.md) records the
 details. No page content was stored, and the live check did not enqueue products
 or persist ingestion run records. Further source requests require explicit
 approval; Phase 2 remains open.
 
 ## Proposed manifest and ingestion contract
 
 * Generate a manifest only from a successfully parsed and deduplicated catalog.
 * Store a manifest version, selection method, selected product identifiers,
   display names, canonical product URLs, and selection timestamp.
 * Reuse the same manifest for normal reruns. Replacing the sample requires an
   explicit operation and a new version.
 * Enqueue one product reference per message. Never place source content or
   credentials in queue messages.
 * Use stable source/document/chunk identifiers and content hashes for
   idempotency. Record product-level success, protected skip, retry, and failure
   outcomes without retaining protected content.
 * Treat changes to source content, parser version, embedding deployment, and
   embedding dimensions as index-versioning events.
 * Define retry, poison-message, deletion, stale-content, and partial-run behavior
   before Phase 2 implementation.
 
 ## Phase 0 exit review
 
 The user approved the proposed Phase 0 direction with amendments and authorized
 Phase 0b. The live feed is now parsed and a manifest is available, but product
 page access remains inconclusive. Ingestion stays gated on source terms,
 validation of the login-content classifications, and Phase 2 approval. The
 original additional GET budget is exhausted; further live requests require
 approval and do not bypass later phase gates.
 
 The full phase gate is listed in the
 [implementation plan](../implementation-plan.md#phase-0-product-discovery-and-architecture-decisions).

# Microsoft Agent Framework Overview | Microsoft Learn

Agent Framework brings together four primary areas:

| - | Description |
| --- | --- |
| **[Agents](../concepts/agents/)** | Individual agents that use LLMs to process inputs, call [tools](../agents/tools/) and [MCP servers](../agents/tools/hosted-mcp-tools), and generate responses. Supports Microsoft Foundry, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, Ollama, and [more](../integrations/by-component/model-providers/). |
| **[Harness Agent](../concepts/harness)** | An opinionated agent with batteries-included capabilities for long, multi-step tasks — planning and todo tracking, context compaction, file access and memory, don't-ask-again tool approval, and observability. |
| **[Workflows](../concepts/workflows/)** | Functional and graph-based workflows that connect agents and functions through explicit execution paths. |
| **[Integrations](../integrations/)** | Connections to model providers, agent services, tools, context providers, middleware, evaluation services, and UI frameworks, organized by provider and component. |

## Understand the code
In Foundry IQ, [filters](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/search/vector-search-filters) apply to nonvector fields in an index. The `Single vector search with filter` cell filters on the `Tags` field to filter out any hotels that don't provide free Wi-Fi.
```python
# vector_query omitted for brevity

results = search_client.search(
    vector_queries=[vector_query],
    filter="Tags/any(tag: tag eq 'free wifi')",
    select=["HotelId", "HotelName", "Description", "Category", "Tags"],
    top=7,
    include_total_count=True
)
```
#### Single vector search with a geo filter
You can specify a [geo-spatial filter](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/search/search-query-odata-geo-spatial-functions) to limit results to a specific geographic area. The `Single vector search with geo filter` cell specifies a geographic point (Washington D.C., using longitude and latitude coordinates) and returns hotels within 300 kilometers. The `vector_filter_mode` parameter determines when the filter runs. In this case, `postFilter` runs the filter after the vector search.
#### Hybrid search
[Hybrid search](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/search/hybrid-search-overview) combines full-text and vector queries in a single request. The `Hybrid search` cell runs both query types concurrently, and then uses Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) to merge the results into a unified ranking. RRF uses the inverse of result rankings from each result set to produce a merged ranking. Notice that hybrid search scores are uniformly smaller than single-query scores.
```python
# vector_query omitted for brevity

results = search_client.search(
    search_text="historic hotel walk to restaurants and shopping",
    vector_queries=[vector_query],
    select=["HotelId", "HotelName", "Description", "Category", "Tags"],
    top=5,
    include_total_count=True
)
```
#### Semantic hybrid search
The `Semantic hybrid search` cell demonstrates [semantic ranking](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/search/semantic-search-overview), which reranks results based on language understanding.
```python
# vector_query omitted for brevity

results = search_client.search(
    search_text="historic hotel walk to restaurants and shopping",
    vector_queries=[vector_query],
    select=["HotelId", "HotelName", "Category", "Description"],
    query_type="semantic",
    semantic_configuration_name="my-semantic-config",
    top=5,
    include_total_count=True
)
```","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/search/search-get-started-vector#understand-the-code"},{"title":"Create a hybrid query in Foundry IQ (Azure AI Search)","content":"# Create a hybrid query in Foundry IQ (Azure AI Search)
## Set up a hybrid query
### **REST**
The following example shows a hybrid query request using the REST API.
This example is from the [vector quickstart](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Azure-Samples/azure-search-rest-samples/refs/heads/main/Quickstart-vectors/az-search-quickstart-vectors.rest) that has vector and nonvector content, and several query examples. For brevity, the vector is truncated in this article.
**Key points:**

## How does hybrid search work?
In a search index, vector fields containing embeddings coexist with textual and numerical fields. You can formulate hybrid queries that execute simultaneously. Hybrid queries take advantage of existing text-based functionality like filtering, faceting, sorting, scoring profiles, and [semantic ranking](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/search/semantic-search-overview) on your text fields, while executing a similarity search against vectors in a single search request.
Hybrid search combines results from both full-text and vector queries, which use different ranking functions such as BM25 for text, and Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) and exhaustive K Nearest Neighbors (eKNN) for vectors. An [RRF](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/search/hybrid-search-ranking) algorithm merges the results. The query response provides just one result set, using RRF to rank the unified results.","contentUrl":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/search/hybrid-search-overview#how-does-hybrid-search-work"},{"title":"Hybrid search using vectors and full-text search in Foundry IQ (Azure AI Search)","content":"# Hybrid search using vectors and full-text search in Foundry IQ (Azure AI Search)
Note
[Foundry IQ (Azure AI Search)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/what-is-foundry-iq) provides direct indexing and query APIs alongside higher-level knowledge source and knowledge base APIs for managed retrieval. Use the [Azure portal](https://portal.azure.com), [REST APIs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/search-api-versions#rest-apis), or [Azure SDKs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/search-api-versions#all-azure-sdks) to configure these capabilities, or connect agents to knowledge bases in the [Microsoft Foundry portal](https://ai.azure.com/?cid=learnDocs).
Hybrid search is a single query request configured for both full-text and vector queries. It runs against a search index that contains searchable, plain-text content and generated embeddings. For query purposes, hybrid search:
1. Is a single query request that includes both `search` and `vectorQueries` query parameters.
2. Runs full-text search and vector search in parallel.
3. Merges results from each query by using [Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/search/hybrid-search-ranking).
This article explains the concepts, benefits, and limitations of hybrid search. Links at the end provide usage instructions and next steps. You can also watch the embedded video for an explanation of how hybrid retrieval contributes to high-quality generative search applications.
## Why use hybrid search?
Hybrid search combines the strengths of vector search and keyword search. The advantage of vector search is finding information that's conceptually similar to your search query, even if there are no keyword matches in the inverted index. The advantage of keyword or full-text search is precision, with the ability to apply optional semantic ranking that improves the quality of the initial results. Some scenarios, such as querying over product codes, highly specialized jargon, dates, and people's names, perform better with keyword search because it can identify exact matches.
Benchmark testing on real-world and benchmark datasets indicates that hybrid retrieval with semantic ranker offers significant benefits in search relevance.

    def create_index_definition(index_name: str, model: str) -> SearchIndex:
        dimensions = 1536  # text-embedding-ada-002
        if model == "text-embedding-3-large":
            dimensions = 3072
    
        # The fields we want to index. The "embedding" field is a vector field that will
        # be used for vector search.
        fields = [
            SimpleField(name="id", type=SearchFieldDataType.String, key=True),
            SearchableField(name="content", type=SearchFieldDataType.String),
            SimpleField(name="filepath", type=SearchFieldDataType.String),
            SearchableField(name="title", type=SearchFieldDataType.String),
            SimpleField(name="url", type=SearchFieldDataType.String),
            SearchField(
                name="contentVector",
                type=SearchFieldDataType.Collection(SearchFieldDataType.Single),
                searchable=True,
                # Size of the vector created by the text-embedding-ada-002 model.
                vector_search_dimensions=dimensions,
                vector_search_profile_name="myHnswProfile",
            ),
        ]
    
        # The "content" field should be prioritized for semantic ranking.
        semantic_config = SemanticConfiguration(
            name="default",
            prioritized_fields=SemanticPrioritizedFields(
                title_field=SemanticField(field_name="title"),
                keywords_fields=[],
                content_fields=[SemanticField(field_name="content")],
            ),
        )
    
        # For vector search, we want to use the HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World)
        # algorithm (a type of approximate nearest neighbor search algorithm) with cosine
        # distance.
        vector_search = VectorSearch(
            algorithms=[
                HnswAlgorithmConfiguration(
                    name="myHnsw",
                    kind=VectorSearchAlgorithmKind.HNSW,
                    parameters=HnswParameters(
                        m=4,
                        ef_construction=1000,
                        ef_search=1000,
                        metric=VectorSearchAlgorithmMetric.COSINE,
                    ),
                ),
                ExhaustiveKnnAlgorithmConfiguration(
                    name="myExhaustiveKnn",
                    kind=VectorSearchAlgorithmKind.EXHAUSTIVE_KNN,
                    parameters=ExhaustiveKnnParameters(metric=VectorSearchAlgorithmMetric.COSINE),
                ),
            ],
            profiles=[
                VectorSearchProfile(
                    name="myHnswProfile",
                    algorithm_configuration_name="myHnsw",
                ),
                VectorSearchProfile(
                    name="myExhaustiveKnnProfile",
                    algorithm_configuration_name="myExhaustiveKnn",
                ),
            ],
        )
    
        # Create the semantic settings with the configuration
        semantic_search = SemanticSearch(configurations=[semantic_config])
    
        # Create the search index definition

from typing import List, Dict, Any
from utils import get_clients, get_clients_passwordless, read_file_return_json, insert_data, print_search_results, drop_vector_indexes
from dotenv import load_dotenv

# Load environment variables
load_dotenv()

def create_hnsw_vector_index(collection, vector_field: str, dimensions: int) -> None:

    print(f"Creating HNSW vector index on field '{vector_field}'...")

    # Drop any existing vector indexes on this field first
    drop_vector_indexes(collection, vector_field)

    # Use the native MongoDB command for DocumentDB vector indexes
    index_command = {
        "createIndexes": collection.name,
        "indexes": [
            {
                "name": f"hnsw_index_{vector_field}",
                "key": {
                    vector_field: "cosmosSearch"  # DocumentDB vector search index type
                },
                "cosmosSearchOptions": {
                    # HNSW algorithm configuration
                    "kind": "vector-hnsw",

                    # Vector dimensions must match the embedding model
                    "dimensions": dimensions,

                    # Cosine similarity works well with text embeddings
                    "similarity": "COS",

                    # Maximum connections per node in the graph (parameter 'm')
                    # Higher values improve recall but increase memory usage and build time
                    "m": 16,

                    # Size of the candidate list during construction
                    # Higher values improve index quality but slow down building
                    "efConstruction": 64
                }
            }
        ]
    }

    try:
        # Execute the createIndexes command directly
        result = collection.database.command(index_command)
        print("HNSW vector index created successfully")

    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error creating HNSW vector index: {e}")
        raise

def perform_hnsw_vector_search(collection,
                              azure_openai_client,
                              query_text: str,
                              vector_field: str,
                              model_name: str,
                              top_k: int = 5,
                              ef_search: int = 16) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:

    print(f"Performing HNSW vector search for: '{query_text}'")

    try:
        # Convert query text to embedding vector
        embedding_response = azure_openai_client.embeddings.create(
            input=[query_text],
            model=model_name
        )

        query_embedding = embedding_response.data[0].embedding

        # Build aggregation pipeline for HNSW vector search
        pipeline = [
            {
                "$search": {
                    # Use cosmosSearch for vector operations in DocumentDB
                    "cosmosSearch": {
                        # Query vector to find similar documents for
                        "vector": query_embedding,

                        # Field in documents containing vectors to compare against
                        "path": vector_field,

                        # Maximum number of results to return
                        "k": top_k
                    }
                }
            },
            {
                # Select only the fields needed for display and add similarity score
                "$project": {
                    "document": "$$ROOT",
                    # Add search score from metadata
                    "score": {"$meta": "searchScore"}
                }
            }
        ]

        # Execute the search pipeline
        results = list(collection.aggregate(pipeline))

        return results

    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error performing HNSW vector search: {e}")
        raise

def main():

    print("Starting HNSW vector search demonstration...")

    # Load configuration from environment variables
    config = {
        'cluster_name': os.getenv('MONGO_CLUSTER_NAME'),
        'database_name': 'Hotels',
        'collection_name': 'hotels_hnsw',
        'data_file': os.getenv('DATA_FILE_WITH_VECTORS', '../data/Hotels_Vector.json'),
        'vector_field': os.getenv('EMBEDDED_FIELD', 'DescriptionVector'),
        'model_name': os.getenv('AZURE_OPENAI_EMBEDDING_MODEL', 'text-embedding-3-small'),
        'dimensions': int(os.getenv('EMBEDDING_DIMENSIONS', '1536')),
        'batch_size': int(os.getenv('LOAD_SIZE_BATCH', '100'))
    }

    try:
        # Initialize MongoDB and Azure OpenAI clients
        print("\nInitializing clients...")
        mongo_client, azure_openai_client = get_clients_passwordless()

        # Access database and collection
        database = mongo_client[config['database_name']]
        collection = database[config['collection_name']]

        # Load hotel data with embeddings
        print(f"\nLoading data from {config['data_file']}...")
        data = read_file_return_json(config['data_file'])
        print(f"Loaded {len(data)} documents")

        # Verify that embeddings are present in the data
        documents_with_embeddings = [doc for doc in data if config['vector_field'] in doc]
        if not documents_with_embeddings:
            raise ValueError(f"No documents found with embeddings in field '{config['vector_field']}'. "
                           "Please run create_embeddings.py first.")

        # Insert data into MongoDB collection
        print(f"\nPreparing collection '{config['collection_name']}'...")

        # Insert hotel data with embeddings
        stats = insert_data(
            collection,
            documents_with_embeddings,
            batch_size=config['batch_size']
        )

        if stats['inserted'] == 0 and not stats.get('skipped'):
            raise ValueError("No documents were inserted successfully")

        # Create HNSW vector index (skip if data was already present)
        if not stats.get('skipped'):
            print("\nCreating HNSW vector index...")
            create_hnsw_vector_index(
                collection,
                config['vector_field'],
                config['dimensions']
            )

            # Allow time for index to become ready
            import time
            print("Waiting for index to be ready...")
            time.sleep(2)

        # Demonstrate HNSW search with various queries
        query = "quintessential lodging near running trails, eateries, retail"

        results = perform_hnsw_vector_search(
            collection,
            azure_openai_client,
            query,
            config['vector_field'],
            config['model_name'],
            top_k=5,
            ef_search=16
        )

        # Display the search results
        print_search_results(results, max_results=5, show_score=True)

    except Exception as e:
        print(f"\nError during HNSW demonstration: {e}")
        raise

    finally:
        # Clean up MongoDB connection
        if 'mongo_client' in locals():
            mongo_client.close()

if __name__ == "__main__":

## Getting started
There are two types of keys used to access your search service: **admin***(read-write)* and **query***(read-only)* keys. Restricting access and operations in client apps is essential to safeguarding the search assets on your service. ```python
from azure.core.credentials import AzureKeyCredential

index_name = os.environ["AZURE_SEARCH_INDEX_NAME"]

 # Python Script Instructions
 
 Conventions for Python 3.11+ scripts used in automation, tooling, and CLI applications.
 
 ## Entry Points and Exit Codes
 
 ```python
 import sys
 
 EXIT_SUCCESS = 0  # Successful execution
 EXIT_FAILURE = 1  # General failure
 EXIT_ERROR = 2    # Arguments or configuration error
 
 
 def main() -> int:
     """Main entry point for the script."""
     return EXIT_SUCCESS
 
 
 if __name__ == "__main__":
     sys.exit(main())
 ```
 
 Standard exit codes: 0 success, 1 failure, 2 configuration error, 130 user interrupt (SIGINT).
 
 ## CLI Argument Parsing
 
 ### argparse
 
 Extract parser creation into a separate function for testability.
 
 ```python
 import argparse
 from pathlib import Path
 
 
 def create_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
     """Create and configure argument parser."""
     parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Process files")
     parser.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true")
     parser.add_argument("-o", "--output", type=Path, default=Path("output.txt"))
     parser.add_argument("input_file", type=Path)
     return parser
 ```
 
 Use `type=Path` for file arguments and `action="store_true"` for boolean flags.
 
 ### click
 
 For complex CLIs with subcommands or interactive prompts, use the *click* framework.
 
 ```python
 import click
 
 
 @click.command()
 @click.option("-v", "--verbose", is_flag=True)
 @click.argument("input_file", type=click.Path(exists=True))
 @click.pass_context
 def main(ctx: click.Context, verbose: bool, input_file: str) -> None:
     """Process input files."""
     ctx.exit(0)  # Explicit exit code
 ```
 
 Use `@click.group()` for subcommands, `ctx.exit(code)` for exit codes, and `ctx.fail(message)` for errors.
 
 ## Logging Configuration
 
 ```python
 import logging
 
 logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
 
 
 def configure_logging(verbose: bool = False) -> None:
     """Configure logging based on verbosity level."""
     level = logging.DEBUG if verbose else logging.INFO
     logging.basicConfig(level=level, format="%(levelname)s: %(message)s")
 ```
 
 Create module-level logger, configure early in main. For file logging, add *FileHandler* to the root logger.
 
 ## Path Handling
 
 Use *pathlib.Path* exclusively; avoid *os.path*.
 
 ```python
 from pathlib import Path
 
 
 def process_file(path: Path) -> None:
     """Read, process, and write file content."""
     content = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
     processed = transform_content(content)
     output_path = path.with_suffix(".out")
     output_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
     output_path.write_text(processed, encoding="utf-8")
 ```
 
 Common patterns: `cwd()`, `resolve()`, `exists()`, `is_dir()`, `is_file()`, `iterdir()`, `glob()`, `rglob()`, `read_text()`, `write_text()`, `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)`, `parent`, `name`, `stem`, `suffix`.
 
 ## Subprocess Execution
 
 Use *subprocess.run()* with error handling.
 
 ```python
 import subprocess
 import os
 from pathlib import Path
 
 
 def run_command(cmd: list[str], cwd: Path | None = None, extra_env: dict[str, str] | None = None) -> str:
     """Run command and return stdout, raising on failure."""
     env = os.environ.copy()
     if extra_env:
         env.update(extra_env)
     try:
         result = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True, cwd=cwd, env=env)
         return result.stdout
     except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
         logger.error("Command failed: %s\nstderr: %s", e.returncode, e.stderr)
         raise
     except FileNotFoundError:
         logger.error("Command not found: %s", cmd[0])
         raise
 ```
 
 Use `capture_output=True` and `text=True` for string output. Use `check=True` to raise on non-zero exit.
 
 ## Type Hints
 
 Use Python 3.11+ syntax with built-in generics.
 
 ```python
 from pathlib import Path
 from typing import Literal, Self
 
 
 def process_items(items: list[str]) -> dict[str, int]:  # Built-in generics
     return {item: len(item) for item in items}
 
 
 def read_file(path: str | Path) -> str:  # Union with pipe
     return Path(path).read_text(encoding="utf-8")
 
 
 def find_config(name: str) -> Path | None:  # Optional with pipe
     config = Path(name)
     return config if config.exists() else None
 
 
 def set_level(level: Literal["debug", "info", "warning"]) -> None:  # Constrained values
     pass
 
 
 class Builder:
     def add(self, item: str) -> Self:  # Fluent interface
         self.items.append(item)
         return self
 ```
 
 Use `list[str]` not `typing.List[str]`, `str | None` not `Optional[str]`, `Literal` for constrained values, `Self` for chained methods.
 
 ## Error Handling
 
 Handle interrupts and pipe errors at the top level.
 
 ```python
 import sys
 
 
 def main() -> int:
     """Main entry point with error handling."""
     try:
         return run()
     except KeyboardInterrupt:
         print("\nInterrupted by user", file=sys.stderr)
         return 130
     except BrokenPipeError:
         sys.stderr.close()
         return 1
     except Exception as e:
         print(f"Error: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
         return 1
 ```
 
 Custom exceptions can carry exit codes:
 
 ```python
 class ScriptError(Exception):
     def __init__(self, message: str, exit_code: int = 1) -> None:
         super().__init__(message)
         self.exit_code = exit_code
 ```
 
 ## Documentation
 
 Use Google-style docstrings with Args, Returns, Raises, and Example sections.
 
 ```python
 def process_data(data: list[str], *, normalize: bool = False) -> dict[str, int]:
     """Process input data and return statistics.
 
     Args:
         data: List of strings to process.
         normalize: If True, normalize values before processing.
 
     Returns:
         Dictionary mapping processed items to their counts.
 
     Raises:
         ValueError: If data is empty.
 
     Example:
         >>> process_data(["a", "b", "a"])
         {'a': 2, 'b': 1}
     """
 ```
 
 Include module docstrings with description, usage, and examples.
 
 ## Script Organization
 
 Organize scripts in this order:
 
 1. Shebang: `#!/usr/bin/env python3`
 2. Copyright header: `# Copyright (c) Microsoft Corporation.`
 3. SPDX license identifier: `# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT`
 4. PEP 723 inline script metadata (if applicable)
 5. Future imports: `from __future__ import annotations`
 6. Imports: standard library, third-party, local (separated by blank lines)
 7. Constants and exit codes
 8. Module-level logger
 9. Helper functions
 10. Parser creation function
 11. Logging configuration function
 12. Run logic function
 13. Main entry point
 14. Module guard: `if __name__ == "__main__": sys.exit(main())`
 
 ## Inline Script Metadata
 
 PEP 723 inline metadata enables automatic dependency installation with *uv*.
 
 ```python
 #!/usr/bin/env python3
 # Copyright (c) Microsoft Corporation.
 # SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
 # /// script
 # requires-python = ">=3.11"
 # dependencies = [
 #     "click>=8.0",
 #     "rich>=13.0",
 # ]
 # ///
 ```
 
 Place after copyright and SPDX headers, before module docstring. Run with `uv run script.py`.

 # UV Environment Management
 
 You are a Python environment specialist focused on uv virtual environment management. Help users create, activate, and manage Python virtual environments using uv commands.
 
 ## Core uv Commands
 
 Use these specific uv commands to manage Python projects:
 
 1. **Initialize new project**: `uv init`
 2. **Create virtual environment**: `uv venv .venv` (done automatically by uv init)
 3. **Add dependencies**: `uv add <package>` (updates pyproject.toml automatically)
 4. **Sync environment**: `uv sync` (installs from pyproject.toml)
 5. **Lock dependencies**: `uv lock` (creates uv.lock file)
 6. **Check installed packages**: `uv pip freeze` (after activating environment)
 7. **Activate environment**: `source .venv/bin/activate`
 
 ## Always Install
 
 Always install the following packages in every virtual environment:
 
 * `ipykernel`
 * `ipywidgets`
 * `ruff`
 * `tqdm`
 * `pytest`
 
 Unless otherwise specified, use Python 3.11.
 
 ## Check CUDA
 
 Check if the current user is running on a CUDA-enabled system:
 
 ```bash
 if command -v nvidia-smi &> /dev/null; then
     CUDA_VERSION=$(nvidia-smi | grep -oP 'CUDA Version: \K[0-9.]+')
     echo $CUDA_VERSION
 fi
 ```
 
 If CUDA is available, and you're asked to install pytorch (don't do it until asked for pytorch), use the following command:
 
 ```bash
 if [[ "$CUDA_VERSION" == "12.8" ]]; then
     uv add torch torchvision torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
 elif [[ "$CUDA_VERSION" == "12.6" ]]; then
     uv add torch torchvision torchaudio
 elif [[ "$CUDA_VERSION" == "11.8" ]]; then
     uv add torch torchvision torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu118
 else
     echo "Detected CUDA version: $CUDA_VERSION"
     echo "Unable to locate the appropriate torch version for CUDA $CUDA_VERSION."
     return 1
 fi
 ```
 
 ## Locking environments and syncing
 
 When the user asks to lock or compile the environment, use the following commands:
 
 ```bash
 # Lock dependencies (creates uv.lock)
 uv lock
 
 # Sync environment from pyproject.toml
 uv sync
 
 # For legacy requirements.txt export (if needed)
 uv pip compile pyproject.toml -o requirements.txt
 ```
 
 ## Your Role
 
 When users request help with Python environments:
 
 1. **Initialize project**: Use `uv init` to create project structure with pyproject.toml
 2. **Add dependencies**: Use `uv add <package>` to add packages (automatically updates pyproject.toml)
 3. **Install default packages**: Add the required packages using `uv add`
 4. **Sync environment**: Use `uv sync` to install dependencies from pyproject.toml
 5. **Lock dependencies**: Use `uv lock` to create reproducible builds
 6. **Show activation**: Explain how to activate with `source .venv/bin/activate`
 7. **Verify installation**: Use `uv pip freeze` to check installed packages
 
 ## Syncing Workflow
 
 **For new projects:**
 
 ```bash
 uv init
 uv add ipykernel ipywidgets ruff tqdm pytest [additional packages]
 uv sync
 uv lock
 ```
 
 **Adding new dependencies:**
 
 ```bash
 uv add <package>  # Automatically updates pyproject.toml and syncs
 ```
 
 Keep responses focused on the modern uv project management approach. Always use `.venv` as the virtual environment directory name.

# Create a hybrid query in Foundry IQ (Azure AI Search)

Note

[Foundry IQ (Azure AI Search)](/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/what-is-foundry-iq) provides direct indexing and query APIs alongside higher-level knowledge source and knowledge base APIs for managed retrieval. Use the [Azure portal](https://portal.azure.com), [REST APIs](/en-us/azure/search/search-api-versions#rest-apis), or [Azure SDKs](/en-us/azure/search/search-api-versions#all-azure-sdks) to configure these capabilities, or connect agents to knowledge bases in the [Microsoft Foundry portal](https://ai.azure.com/?cid=learnDocs).

Important

Features or capabilities marked (preview) in this article are in Public Preview and are subject to the [Supplemental Terms of Use for Microsoft Azure Previews](https://azure.microsoft.com/support/legal/preview-supplemental-terms/). For preview terms specific to Foundry IQ (Azure AI Search), see [Preview functionality](search-feature-terms#preview-functionality).

[Hybrid search](hybrid-search-overview) combines text (keyword) and vector queries in a single search request. Both queries execute in parallel. The results are merged and reordered by new search scores, using [Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)](hybrid-search-ranking) to return a unified result set. In many cases, [per benchmark tests](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/azure-ai-foundry-blog/azure-ai-search-outperforming-vector-search-with-hybrid-retrieval-and-reranking/3929167), hybrid queries with semantic ranking return the most relevant results.

In this article, learn how to:

- Set up a basic hybrid request
- Add parameters and filters
- Improve relevance using semantic ranking or vector weights
- Optimize query behaviors by controlling inputs (`maxTextRecallSize`)

By the end of this article, you can execute hybrid queries that combine keyword and vector search with optional semantic ranking.

## Prerequisites

- An Azure subscription. [Create one for free](https://azure.microsoft.com/pricing/purchase-options/azure-account?cid=msft_learn).
- A Foundry IQ (Azure AI Search) service. [Create a service](search-create-service-portal) or [find an existing service](https://portal.azure.com/#blade/HubsExtension/BrowseResourceBlade/resourceType/Microsoft.Search%2FsearchServices).
- A search index containing `searchable` vector and nonvector fields. We recommend the [**Import data** wizard](search-import-data-portal) to create an index quickly. Otherwise, see [Create an index](search-how-to-create-search-index) and [Add vector fields to a search index](vector-search-how-to-create-index).
- **Permissions**: You need **Search Index Data Reader** to query an index. To create or update an index, you need **Search Index Data Contributor**. For more information, see [Connect using roles](search-security-rbac).
- **(Optional) SDK installation**:

    - Python: `pip install azure-search-documents`
    - C#: `dotnet add package Azure.Search.Documents`
- (Optional) If you want built-in text-to-vector conversion of a query string, [create and assign a vectorizer](vector-search-how-to-configure-vectorizer) to vector fields in the search index.

## Choose an API, tool, and workable pattern

- Search Explorer in the Azure portal (supports both stable and preview API search syntax) has a JSON view that lets you paste in a hybrid request.
- Newer stable or preview packages of the Azure SDKs (see change logs for SDK feature support).
- [Stable REST APIs](/en-us/rest/api/searchservice/documents/search-post) or a recent preview API version if you're using preview features like maxTextRecallSize and countAndFacetMode (preview).

    For readability, we use REST examples to explain how the APIs work. You can use a REST client like Visual Studio Code with the REST extension to build hybrid queries. You can also use the Azure SDKs. For more information, see [Quickstart: Vector search](search-get-started-vector).

### Workable hybrid patterns

If you're new to hybrid search, pick one pattern and tune in small steps. Don't start with maximum vector recall, large text recall, and semantic reranking in the same request.

- **Balanced hybrid (default)**: Use this first for most workloads. Start with `k` in the 30 to 50 range, `top` in the 10 to 20 range, and enable semantic ranking only when it improves measured relevance.
- **Recall-first hybrid**: Use this for difficult queries where coverage is the goal. Increase `maxTextRecallSize` gradually and keep vector settings moderate. Expect higher merge cost.
- **Precision-first hybrid**: Use this for low latency at scale. Keep `k` and `top` modest, apply selective filters, and avoid semantic features that don't add value.

### Why overloaded queries throttle

Hybrid queries run text and vector retrieval in parallel and then merge results with RRF. If you increase lexical contribution (for example, by changing hybrid weighting in favor of BM25), you increase the number of text candidates that must be merged with vector candidates. If you combine this with expensive vector settings and semantic reranking, CPU and memory pressure rises quickly.

On smaller capacity configurations, this extra merge and rerank work can cause:

- Higher latency and p95/p99 spikes
- 429 throttling responses
- Client-observed dropped or timed-out requests when retry behavior isn't configured

### Tuning order before scaling out

Tune query and vector settings before you add replicas:

1. Reduce expensive vector search settings first. For example, if `efSearch` and `maxConnections` are set aggressively, lower them before scaling out (for example, reduce `efSearch` from around 800 to 128 to 192, and reduce `maxConnections` from 64 to 32).
2. Limit semantic reranking scope to cases that benefit from it.
3. Re-test latency and 429 rates under representative load.
4. Scale replicas only if throttling persists after tuning.

Use this sequence to improve stability first and control cost before you scale.

Both `k` and `top` are optional. Unspecified, the default number of results in a response is 50. You can set `top` and `skip` to [page through more results](search-pagination-page-layout#paging-results) or change the default.

Note

If you're using hybrid search in 2024-05-01-preview API, you can control the number of results from the keyword query using maxTextRecallSize. Combine this with a setting for `k` to control the representation from each search subsystem (keyword and vector).

### Semantic ranker results

Note

The semantic ranker can take up to 50 results.

If you're using semantic ranker in 2024-05-01-preview or later, it's a best practice to set `k` and `maxTextRecallSize` to sum to at least 50 total. You can then restrict the results returned to the user with the `top` parameter.

If you're using semantic ranker in an API version earlier than 2024-05-01-preview, follow these steps:

- For keyword-only search (no vectors) set `top` to 50
- For hybrid search set `k` to 50, to ensure that the semantic ranker gets at least 50 results.

### Ranking

Multiple sets are created for hybrid queries, with or without the optional [semantic reranking](semantic-search-overview). Ranking of results is computed by Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF).

In this section, compare the responses between single vector search and simple hybrid search for the top result. The different ranking algorithms, HNSW's similarity metric and RRF is this case, produce scores that have different magnitudes. This behavior is by design. RRF scores can appear quite low, even with a high similarity match. Lower scores are a characteristic of the RRF algorithm. In a hybrid query with RRF, more of the reciprocal of the ranked documents are included in the results, given the relatively smaller score of the RRF ranked documents, as opposed to pure vector search.

**Single Vector Search**: @search.score for results ordered by cosine similarity (default vector similarity distance function).

```json
{
    "@search.score": 0.8399121,
    "HotelId": "49",
    "HotelName": "Swirling Currents Hotel",
    "Description": "Spacious rooms, glamorous suites and residences, rooftop pool, walking access to shopping, dining, entertainment and the city center.",
    "Category": "Luxury",
    "Address": {
    "City": "Arlington"
    }
}
```

**Hybrid Search**: @search.score for hybrid results ranked using Reciprocal Rank Fusion.

```json
{
    "@search.score": 0.032786883413791656,
    "HotelId": "49",
    "HotelName": "Swirling Currents Hotel",
    "Description": "Spacious rooms, glamorous suites and residences, rooftop pool, walking access to shopping, dining, entertainment and the city center.",
    "Category": "Luxury",
    "Address": {
    "City": "Arlington"
    }
}
```

## Troubleshoot hybrid queries

Use the following table to diagnose common issues with hybrid queries.

| Issue | Possible cause | Resolution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Empty results | Vector field name mismatch or missing index data | Verify `fields` in `vectorQueries` matches a vector field in your index schema. Check that documents contain vector data. |
| Low RRF scores | Normal RRF behavior | RRF scores are inherently lower than similarity scores. A score of 0.03 can still indicate a strong match. |
| Vector results dominate | Text query underperforming | Increase `maxTextRecallSize` to include more BM25 results, or adjust vector weighting. |
| Text results dominate | Vector similarity too low | Check embedding quality. Ensure query vector uses the same model as document vectors. |
| Semantic ranker returns fewer results | Insufficient input documents | Set `k` to at least 50 when using semantic ranking. Check that filters aren't too restrictive. |
| Filter not applied to vectors | Using global filter only | For vector-specific filtering, use `filterOverride` in the vector query (preview). |
| Unexpected field in results | `select` parameter missing | Add `select` to specify which fields to return. Exclude vector fields for readability. |
